title: Frequency- and Power-Dependent Optical Response of a Cesium Rydberg Microwave Receiver
authors: Jure Pirman, Ema Stopar, Katja Gosar, Erik Zupanič, Peter Jeglič
abstract: We show experimentally obtained frequency- and power-dependent optical response of a room-temperature cesium vapor cell used as a Rydberg microwave receiver based on electromagnetically induced transparency. An applied microwave field couples the ${70S_{1/2}}$ Rydberg state to the nearby ${70P_{1/2}}$, ${70P_{3/2}}$, ${69P_{1/2}}$, and ${69P_{3/2}}$ states, modifying the probe-transmission spectrum. Probe transmission is recorded over a 800 MHz range of coupling laser detunings. These EIT spectra are measured for RF frequencies from 9 to 13.5 GHz and over a 40 dB range of RF power. We analyze the RF induced splittings in the recorded EIT spectra. We observe both limiting cases, where the EIT peak separation is either dominated by the RF detuning or by the RF power. At higher powers we are also able to observe complex features due to coupling of multiple nearby Rydberg states. We further analyze the probe-transmission signal at zero coupling-laser detuning. Sigmoidal fits to the power-response curves are used to determine the midpoint power and the 10-90% transition interval as functions of RF frequency.
summary: This paper experimentally characterizes a cesium vapor cell acting as a Rydberg microwave receiver using Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT). By measuring the optical response across varying microwave frequencies and powers, the authors map out the system's frequency- and power-dependent behavior. This demonstrates the feasibility of using Rydberg atoms for high-sensitivity radio frequency sensing and metrology.
main_problem: To experimentally investigate the frequency- and power-dependent optical response of a room-temperature cesium vapor cell used as a Rydberg microwave receiver.
main_result: The experiment successfully characterized the system's response across various RF frequencies and power levels, resolving multiple Rydberg-Rydberg transitions and demonstrating its potential as a high-sensitivity RF sensor.
method: The study measures probe transmission through the vapor cell while sweeping the microwave frequency and applied RF power, analyzing the resulting Electromagnetically Induced Transparency (EIT) spectra.
model_or_system: The system utilizes Cesium atoms in a Rydberg state within an EIT configuration. The microwave field couples the $70S_{1/2}$ state to nearby P-states, and the response is analyzed using a driven two-level system model.
key_observables: EIT spectra, peak separation ($\Delta_f$), midpoint power ($P_0$), and transition frequency ($f_0$).
important_parameters: RF frequencies (9 to 13.5 GHz), RF power (40 dB range), and coupling laser detuning ($\Delta_c$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the two-level model for microwave coupling, and the measurements are performed without active magnetic-field compensation.
figures_summary: Figures show normalized EIT signals at different RF powers across varying frequencies, and plots detail the dependence of the peak splitting ($\Delta_f$) on both RF power and detuning.
paper_structure: The paper details the experimental setup, presents measurements of the EIT spectra across a wide parameter space, analyzes the resulting spectral splittings in different power regimes, and characterizes the power-dependent response using sigmoidal fitting.
why_interesting: This work provides a concrete, measurable platform for studying nonlinear quantum optics effects (EIT) driven by microwave fields, offering insights into how external fields modify atomic energy level couplings in Rydberg systems.
